### Summary
`ed25519.verify()` does not reject public keys of small order, such as the identity point. Under such a key, a signature with `S = 0` and a small-order `R` verifies for many messages, or for every message with the identity key, without any private key. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`crypto_sign_open()` in `lib/ed25519.js` decodes the public key `A` with `unpackneg()`, which only checks that the point is on the curve, and then checks `R == [S]B - [k]A` with `k = SHA-512(R || A || M)`. Nothing rejects public keys of small order: the identity point, the other 7 points of order 2, 4 or 8, and their non-canonical encodings with `y >= p`.

With `S = 0`, the check becomes `R == [k](-A)`. For a small-order `A`, `[k](-A)` is one of at most 8 small-order points, so an attacker can make a valid signature by trying the small-order values of `R`. For the identity key (`01 00 … 00`), `R = identity` and `S = 0` verifies for every message. For the other small-order keys, a given message can be forged with high probability. No private key is involved. The `S < L` check added for CVE-2026-33895 (GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw) doesn't apply, because `S = 0` is canonical.

Keys produced by Ed25519 key generation (`ed25519.generateKeyPair()` or any RFC 8032 implementation) are never small-order, so signatures under them cannot be forged this way. Applications are affected when they verify signatures against a public key an attacker can choose (for example a key included with the signed data, a self-registered key, or a key in an attacker-controlled document) and rely on the signature being bound to the message: proof of possession, attribution, non-repudiation or deduplication.

RFC 8032 doesn't require rejecting small-order public keys, and implementations differ. libsodium rejects them, and Node.js `crypto.verify()` (OpenSSL) rejects these signatures.

The fix rejects a public key `A` when `[8]A` is the identity point. This covers all small-order points and their non-canonical encodings.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3. `ed25519.verify()` returns `false` for small-order public keys.

#### Workarounds
Before calling `ed25519.verify()` with a public key from untrusted input, reject keys whose 32-byte encoding is one of the small-order points (the identity `01 00 … 00` and the other encodings that libsodium blocks), or only verify against keys you generated or have otherwise validated.

#### Resources
- RFC 8032, Section 5.1.7 (Ed25519 verification): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8032#section-5.1.7
- GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw / CVE-2026-33895 (a different Ed25519 verification issue, fixed in 1.4.0): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-q67f-28xg-22rw

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)
CVSS 4.0 rates this Moderate because its integrity weighting is higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @analisaperlengkapan.

### Proof of concept
Identity public key `A = 01 00 … 00` (32 bytes) and signature `R = 01 00 … 00`, `S = 00 … 00` (64 bytes):

    forge.ed25519.verify({message: 'admin=true', encoding: 'utf8',
      signature: SIG, publicKey: IDENTITY});
    // <= 1.4.2: true for any message; node:crypto.verify(): false
    // 1.4.3: false

Other small-order public keys (orders 2, 4 and 8, and non-canonical encodings) give forgeries for many messages with `S = 0` and a small-order `R`.

Regression tests are in tests/unit/ed25519.js, and the reporter's PoC is in tests/pocs/ghsa-6889-vf6x-f3g5.js.

### Impact
Applications that verify Ed25519 signatures with node-forge against a public key that an attacker can choose are affected. An attacker can provide a small-order public key and then produce signatures that verify for many or all messages without a private key, defeating checks that rely on a signature being bound to its message under that key (proof of possession, attribution, non-repudiation, deduplication). Signatures under keys from honest key generation cannot be forged, and applications that only verify against their own or otherwise trusted keys are not affected.
1246031.title: Forge: Ed25519 signature verification accepts small-order public keys

1246032.overview:
### Summary
A `forge.tls` client accepts any compression method in the ServerHello, although it only offers no compression. An unknown method makes `connection.process()` throw an uncaught `Error` when the client handles ServerHelloDone, before the server is authenticated. A malicious server or an on-path attacker can use this to terminate a Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
The client's ClientHello offers only the `null` compression method. `tls.parseHelloMessage()` in `lib/tls.js` stores the ServerHello's `compression_method` for the client without checking it (the code has a `TODO: handle compression methods`). When the client handles ServerHelloDone it calls `tls.createConnectionState()`, which throws `Error('Unsupported compression algorithm.')` for any method other than `null` (0) and `deflate` (1). The exception propagates out of `connection.process()`.

The ServerHello isn't authenticated until the server's Finished message, so an on-path attacker can change the compression byte of a genuine ServerHello; the certificate chain still verifies. Applications that pass socket data to `process()` without catching exceptions terminate. This includes `forge.tls.wrapSocket`, which calls `process()` from its socket data handler, and `forge.http`, which uses it. A `deflate` (1) method, also never offered, makes the handshake fail later with an error instead of a crash.

Servers are not affected: a server always selects no compression.

The fix fails the handshake with an `illegal_parameter` alert, through the connection's `error` callback, when the ServerHello selects any compression method other than `null`.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Catch exceptions thrown by `connection.process()` and close the socket.

#### Resources
- RFC 5246, section 7.4.1.3 (Server Hello): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246#section-7.4.1.3
- Related: GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h (another TLS client crash during the handshake, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @alienkeric.

### Proof of concept
A server (or on-path attacker) sends a ServerHello with `compression_method` 0xff, followed by a valid Certificate and ServerHelloDone:

    client.handshake();
    client.process(serverHello + certificate + serverHelloDone);
    // <= 1.4.2: throws Error: Unsupported compression algorithm.
    // 1.4.3: error callback with "Unsupported compression method."

The reporter's PoC (a CA-issued server certificate and the default verify callback) is in tests/pocs/ghsa-w4xr-hqv8-ch44.js, and regression tests are in tests/unit/tls.js.

### Impact
Applications that use `forge.tls` as a client (directly, through `forge.tls.wrapSocket`, or through `forge.http`) and pass data from a network socket to `connection.process()` are affected. The server they connect to, or an on-path attacker, can make `process()` throw before the server is authenticated; if the application doesn't catch it, the Node.js process terminates, dropping all its connections. Servers built on `forge.tls` are not affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.
1246032.title: Forge: TLS client crash on an unsupported ServerHello compression method

1246033.overview:
`forge.http` trims response header and `Set-Cookie` values with the regular expression `/\s*$/`, which takes quadratic time on a long run of whitespace followed by another character. A server or on-path attacker can block a `forge.http` client for minutes with one large response header. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`_trimString()` in `lib/http.js` removes trailing whitespace with `str.replace(/\s*$/, '')`. On a string of n whitespace characters followed by a non-whitespace character, the regular expression engine tries a match at each of the n positions and scans the rest of the run each time, so the work is O(n^2). `forge.http` calls `_trimString()` on every response header value read by `response.readHeader()`, and again on cookie names and values in `response.getCookies()`. There is no limit on header size.

With Node.js 24, an 80 KB header value takes about 4 seconds to parse, and 1 MB about 10 minutes, during which the event loop (or browser tab) is blocked.

`forge.http` is not loaded by `require('node-forge')`. It is part of the `forge.all` bundle and needs a socket pool provided by the application (historically Flash sockets via `forge.xhr`), so few applications use it.

The fix trims trailing whitespace with a loop, as `lib/pem.js` has done since 1.4.1. The trimmed result is unchanged.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Limit the size of HTTP response headers before passing them to `forge.http`, for example in the socket pool's data handler.

#### Resources
- Related: GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x (ReDoS in PEM decoding, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-7wch-p9px-956x

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @manus-pi.

### Proof of concept
    var response = forge.http.createResponse();
    var ws = new Array(40001).join('\t ');
    response.readHeader(forge.util.createBuffer(
      'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nX-A: a' + ws + 'X\r\n\r\n'));
    // <= 1.4.2: about 4 seconds (quadratic in the whitespace length)
    // 1.4.3: about 1 ms

Regression tests are in tests/security/ghsa-6cv4-p8m7-4r25.js.

### Impact
Applications that use `forge.http` to talk to servers they don't control are affected. The server, or an on-path attacker, can send a response header that blocks the client's event loop for minutes, denying service to everything else in the process. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.
1246033.title: Forge: ReDoS in forge.http response header and cookie trimming

1246034.overview:
### Summary
A `forge.tls` client throws an uncaught `TypeError` from `connection.process()` when it receives a ServerHello while it has no session: after a `close_notify` alert or a call to `close()`, or before `handshake()` is called. A malicious server or an on-path attacker can use this to terminate a Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

### Details
`tls.handleHandshake()` in `lib/tls.js` updates the handshake digests with `c.session.md5.update(bytes)` before it calls the message handler. A client creates its session in `handshake()`, and `c.reset()` sets it to `null` when the connection is closed. Closing doesn't set the fail flag, and the client goes back to expecting a ServerHello, so a Handshake record received afterwards still reaches `handleHandshake()`, which throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'md5')`.

This happens:
- after the server sends a `close_notify` alert (at any alert level);
- after the application calls `close()`;
- before the application calls `handshake()`.

The exception propagates out of `connection.process()`. Applications that pass socket data to `process()` from a `data` event handler without catching exceptions, as in the README example, terminate. After a reset the connection uses no encryption, so an on-path attacker can inject the records even when the real server is honest.

Servers are not affected: a server creates its session when it receives a ClientHello.

The fix handles these records like other unexpected records on a closed client: they are ignored.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.3.

#### Workarounds
Catch exceptions thrown by `connection.process()` and close the socket, or stop passing socket data to `process()` once the `closed` callback has been called and until `handshake()` is called again.

#### Resources
- RFC 5246, section 7.2.1 (Closure Alerts): https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5246#section-7.2.1
- Related: GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h (another TLS client `TypeError`, fixed in 1.4.1): https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-525v-9gp9-w22h

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 has no counterpart to 3.1's AC:H beyond AT:P and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by @manus-use.

### Proof of concept
    var c = forge.tls.createConnection({server: false, ...});
    c.handshake();
    // warning close_notify alert, then an empty ServerHello, in separate
    // process() calls
    c.process(forge.util.hexToBytes('15030100020100'));
    c.process(forge.util.hexToBytes('160301000402000000'));
    // <= 1.4.2: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'md5')
    // 1.4.3: the record is ignored

The reporter's PoC is in tests/pocs/ghsa-j8rw-jp99-435v.js, and regression tests are in tests/unit/tls.js.

### Impact
Applications that use `forge.tls` as a client and pass data from a network socket to `connection.process()` are affected. The server they connect to, or an on-path attacker, can make `process()` throw; if the application doesn't catch it, the Node.js process terminates, dropping all its connections. Servers built on `forge.tls` are not affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.
